title: API 653 Training in Denver: Tank Inspector Exam Prep Online
description: Self-paced API 653 exam prep for Denver tank inspectors: Commerce City terminals, airport fuel storage, DJ Basin crude tanks, breakout tanks, cold weather.
h1: API 653 Training in Denver: Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector Exam Prep for Terminal, Refinery, Airport and Midstream Tank Work
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors from Denver to the DJ Basin

Storage tanks around Denver come in more varieties than a single-refinery state suggests. There are refinery and product terminal tanks in Commerce City, airport fuel tanks at Denver International Airport, large crude tanks at stabilization facilities and pipeline origins in Weld County, and many small production tanks on oil and gas locations. They are not all governed by the same rules, and not all of them are API 653 tanks. A Denver candidate who understands which is which goes into the tank inspector examination with an advantage, because the exam keeps returning to scope, applicability and the boundary between API 650 and API 653.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Denver. The API 653 course is studied online at your own pace, with an instructor who answers your questions as you work through the standards. The American Petroleum Institute decides eligibility under Annex D of API 653, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification to those who pass. Taking the course does not shorten or replace any of those steps.

Tanks along Commerce City's fuel corridor

Suncor's refinery on Brighton Boulevard in Commerce City buys crude from the DJ Basin and also receives crude through its transmission system from a storage facility at Guernsey, Wyoming. Its products include gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and paving asphalt, and EIA's 2026 capacity survey credits Colorado, meaning this one refinery, with 13,200 barrels per stream day of asphalt and road oil production capacity. That product list is a tank list too: crude receipt tanks, intermediate and blend tanks, light product tanks and heated asphalt tanks, each with different damage and inspection concerns.

Product moves on to nearby terminals. Sunoco LP's Denver terminal at 3601 East 56th Street in Commerce City, for example, lists 110,000 barrels of storage in nine tanks for gasoline, distillate and ethanol. It lists receipts by pipeline and from the Suncor refinery, with ethanol arriving by truck, and loads trucks at a two-bay rack with automated bottom loading and a vapor combustor. Bulk storage tanks of that size are generally field-erected, which is where API 653 formal inspections are most often called for under the federal spill rule described below.

Fuel storage at Denver International Airport

The airport is a tank site in its own right. DEN's jet fueling design standards manual refers to existing fuel storage tanks numbered 1 to 6 and sets the standards designers must follow for new tanks, among them API 650 for design and construction, API 2350 for overfill protection, API 2000 for venting and API RP 652 for internal coatings; it also cites API RP 651 for cathodic protection and requires leak detection on every aboveground fuel storage tank. Two of those publications, RP 651 and RP 652, are on the API 653 exam. The manual addresses design rather than in-service inspection, which is where an API 653 inspector's work begins once a tank is in service.

Supply into the airport is growing. ONEOK announced in 2024 a 230-mile, 16-inch refined products pipeline from Scott City, Kansas, to the airport, adding 35,000 barrels a day to its Denver-area system, and trade press reported in August 2026 that the expansion was in service.

Crude tanks in Weld County

Some DJ Basin crude has a high vapor pressure, and Western Midstream gathers such crude from the Wattenberg field into its Central Oil Stabilization Facility, which it says includes two 250,000-barrel oil storage tanks and connects to local storage owned by Energy Transfer. Crude then leaves the basin for Cushing on systems such as Saddlehorn and Grand Mesa, White Cliffs and Pony Express, and breakout tanks on pipeline systems fall under federal pipeline safety rules.

Not every operator stores oil at the well. Oxy describes its DJ Basin design as tankless: pipelines rather than trucks carry oil to a central processing facility, eliminating storage tanks near wells, and its operations centre monitors many wells, water tanks and gathering systems remotely. For tank inspectors, a design like that moves storage away from individual pads and toward central facilities.

Which rule brings an API 653 inspector to a Colorado tank

The exam does not test Colorado regulations, but knowing why a tank is inspected helps you answer applicability questions and helps your career.

Kind of tankRule that drives inspectionWhat it asks for
Bulk oil storage at refineries, terminals and other onshore facilitiesEPA's SPCC rule, 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6)Integrity testing on a regular schedule and after material repairs, to an industry standard; EPA's fact sheet points to API 653 for field-erected tanks and says formal API 653 inspections require an API 653 certified inspector
Tanks at onshore oil production facilities40 CFR 112.9(c)(3)Periodic, scheduled visual inspection of each container; EPA's fact sheet points to API RP 12R1 for production tanks
Pipeline breakout tanks49 CFR 195.432Atmospheric and low-pressure steel tanks inspected to API 653 under paragraph (b), without its risk-based internal interval procedure; tanks built to API 2510 inspected under paragraph (c); the yearly inspection in paragraph (a) applies to breakout tanks not covered by (b) or (c)
Smaller petroleum tanksColorado Division of Oil and Public Safety, 7 CCR 1101-14The Division regulates petroleum aboveground tanks holding between 660 and 40,000 gallons, and its periodic formal inspection worksheet follows STI SP001 while asking for the dates of any earlier STI SP001 or API 653 formal inspections

PHMSA proposed in June 2026 to allow risk-based internal inspection intervals for breakout tanks within maximum limits. Until a final rule is published, paragraph (b) stands as written.

Cold, ethanol and soil on the effectivity sheet

The Publications Effectivity Sheet for the March 2027, July 2027 and November 2027 windows lists API 653, 5th edition (November 2014) with Addenda 1 to 4 and two errata; API 650, 14th edition (August 2025); RP 575, 5th edition, with two addenda; RP 651, 5th edition (August 2024); RP 652, 6th edition (December 2025); RP 577; selected sections of RP 576; and the 2025 ASME Section V and Section IX. Its RP 571 list reads almost like a Front Range tank survey:

  • Brittle fracture. Older tanks in a cold climate are the classic case. API 653's brittle fracture chapter, which in the publicly available 2003 edition takes the form of a decision tree, asks whether the tank meets later API 650 toughness rules, whether it has passed a hydrostatic test, how thick its shell is and whether it has already operated safely at the lowest temperature and fill it will see. A change of service to a lower temperature calls for a fresh assessment.
  • Ethanol stress corrosion cracking. Terminals that receive and store fuel ethanol, as the Commerce City terminal above does, are exactly where this mechanism matters.
  • Soil corrosion, microbiologically influenced corrosion and concentration cell corrosion. These govern bottom-side and product-side floor loss, and they are why RP 651 on cathodic protection and RP 652 on bottom linings sit on the sheet.
  • Corrosion under insulation, caustic corrosion and caustic cracking, atmospheric corrosion and sulfuric acid corrosion complete the list. Heated, insulated asphalt tanks make CUI more than a theoretical topic in Colorado.

Worked example: a locally thinned area on a first-course plate

A frequent open-book task is to judge a corroded area on a shell course. The method below follows the shell evaluation paragraphs of API 653; the formulas appear in the publicly available 2003 edition, and you should confirm the paragraph numbers in the edition on your effectivity sheet.

  1. A tank storing denatured ethanol has a nominal diameter D of 100 ft. In a corroded patch on the first course, the least thickness, excluding widely scattered pits, is t2 = 0.36 in.
  2. Critical length: L = 3.7 √(D × t2) = 3.7 × √(100 × 0.36) = 3.7 × 6 = 22.2 in., which is under the 40 in. cap.
  3. Five equally spaced readings along L in the worst vertical plane average t1 = 0.41 in.
  4. For a locally thinned area, tmin = 2.6 H D G ÷ (S E). Take H = 38 ft from the bottom of L to the maximum liquid level, G = 0.79 for the product, S = 24,000 psi and E = 1.0, all as given in the question. Then tmin = (2.6 × 38 × 100 × 0.79) ÷ 24,000 = 7,805 ÷ 24,000 = 0.325 in.
  5. Acceptance: t1 must be at least tmin, and t2 at least 60% of tmin, which is 0.195 in. Both pass.
  6. Now add the corrosion expected before the next inspection. At 0.004 in. a year over five years that is 0.020 in., so the targets become 0.345 in. for t1 and 0.215 in. for t2. The patch still passes; at a higher rate or a longer interval it might not.

Candidates often forget the last step, or use H to the bottom of the course instead of to the bottom of L. Ethanol's lower specific gravity also catches people who reuse a water-filled hydrotest case without changing G.

Routes into API 653 for Denver tank people

Eligibility combines education with tank-related experience in the last 10 years under an authorized inspection agency, set out in API 653's Annex D and summarised on the API 653 certification requirements page. Locally, candidates often come from MFL floor scanning and UT thickness crews who work terminal and refinery outages, from tank construction and repair welders, including graduates of the welding programme at Red Rocks Community College in Lakewood, and from terminal operations staff moving into inspection. Experience on production tanks at oil and gas locations is worth describing carefully, because those tanks are generally not built to API 650 and the application asks what you actually inspected. For a broader primer, read the API 653 tank inspection guide.

Studying API 653 around Front Range tank seasons

Tank work outdoors favours the warmer months, and winter often brings indoor time, which makes it a natural study season for many Denver candidates. Work through API 653 and API 650 together, because so many questions sit on the line between them; then the RP 571 mechanisms on the sheet; then timed practice papers. Prometric lists test centres in and around Denver for the in-person exam day.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Denver terminal or contractor

Terminal operators, refinery tank groups, airport fuel system operators and inspection contractors can enrol several staff at once, each studying at their own pace. Fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API individually, and a sponsor can help most by confirming that the experience described on each application matches the tanks and duties involved.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 course I can attend in person in Denver or Commerce City?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Denver, Commerce City or elsewhere in Colorado; the API 653 course is online and self-paced with instructor Q&A. You go in person only for the examination, which API runs at Prometric test centres after accepting your application. Prometric lists centres in and around Denver.

faq.q: Do terminal tanks in Commerce City need an API 653 certified inspector?
faq.a: That depends on the facility's SPCC plan, which identifies the industry standard it follows and the qualifications that standard requires. EPA's integrity testing fact sheet notes that API 653 is typically used for field-erected tanks and that formal API 653 inspections require an API 653 certified inspector. Routine visual checks can often be done by trained facility staff.

faq.q: Are DJ Basin production tanks API 653 tanks?
faq.a: Generally not. API 653 is written for tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor API 12C, and production tanks are usually built to other specifications. SPCC treats onshore production facilities separately, requiring scheduled visual inspection under 112.9(c)(3), and EPA points to API RP 12R1 for them. Large crude tanks at stabilization facilities and pipeline terminals are a different matter.

faq.q: Does Colorado's tank program require API 653 inspections?
faq.a: Colorado's Division of Oil and Public Safety regulates petroleum aboveground tanks holding between 660 and 40,000 gallons, and its periodic formal inspection worksheet is built around STI SP001, with space for earlier STI SP001 or API 653 formal inspection records. Larger tanks fall outside that size range, so their inspection is usually driven by federal rules such as SPCC and by owner practice.

faq.q: Which brittle fracture rules matter for a tank on the Front Range?
faq.a: API 653's brittle fracture chapter, which works through the tank's construction standard, hydrotest history, shell thickness and service experience, plus API 650's link between design metal temperature and the site's lowest one-day mean ambient temperature. Brittle fracture is also on the examined RP 571 list, so expect questions from both directions.

faq.q: I work at a Commerce City terminal that handles fuel ethanol. Will ethanol cracking come up on the exam?
faq.a: It can. The effectivity sheet for the March, July and November 2027 windows lists ethanol stress corrosion cracking among the RP 571 sections examined. If you inspect terminals that receive fuel ethanol, learn the mechanism's conditions, the equipment it affects and the inspection methods RP 571 describes, then practise finding them quickly.

faq.q: Can a breakout tank at a Colorado pipeline terminal use API 653's risk-based internal interval?
faq.a: Not under the current rule. 49 CFR 195.432(b) requires atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks to be inspected to API 653 but excludes its risk-based procedure for internal inspection intervals. PHMSA published a proposal in June 2026 that would allow RBI intervals within maximum limits, but it does not change the requirement unless and until a final rule is issued.

faq.q: Can a Denver contractor enrol its MFL and UT crew for API 653 preparation?
faq.a: Yes. Contractors and terminal operators can enrol a group, with each person studying at their own pace and asking the instructor questions. Fees are quoted on request. Each candidate needs qualifying experience and an individual application to API, so check eligibility before enrolling anyone who is new to tank work.
